title: Pinch pot whale sea-life figurine
subtitle: A whale in air-dry clay formed from two joined pinch pots
excerpt: A blue whale figurine about 16 cm from nose to tail is built from two joined pinch pots forming the body, with a shaped tail fluke, two pectoral fins, and a dorsal fin pressed in from flat clay. No kiln is needed: the piece dries at room temperature and sits as a shelf display.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. Pinch-pot figurine construction is a traditional hand-building approach. V&A open-access collection for historical ceramic sea-life figurine form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A form made by pressing the thumb into a ball of clay and pinching the walls outward between thumb and forefinger
The joining method: roughen both clay surfaces with a needle, apply clay slip, then press together
The drying stage where clay holds its shape firmly but remains damp enough to refine and add attachments
Fully air-dried and unfired; ready for painting and sealing
A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used here to cut the fin and tail shapes

content.text: A whale figurine about 16 cm nose to tail and 8 cm at its widest sits as a display piece on a shelf or windowsill. The main body is two
pinch pot
halves joined at the centre belly seam, shaped into an elongated form at the front and a tapered tail section at the rear. A flat tail fluke, two pectoral fins, and a dorsal fin are cut from a thin
slab
and attached. No kiln is needed: the figurine dries at room temperature over two days.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body thinned with water)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (for sealing)

content.text: Preparation

Prepare clay slip before starting. Keep all clay not currently in use in a sealed bag. Work quickly: air-dry clay stiffens within 30 to 40 minutes in a dry room. Have the template shapes for the fins and tail drawn on card and ready to cut around before forming the body.
Forming the body halves

Divide 240 g of clay into two equal portions of 120 g each. Roll each into a ball. Form the first pinch pot: press your thumb into the centre of the ball about halfway through, then pinch outward between thumb and forefinger, rotating a quarter-turn between pinches. Aim for a deep bowl shape, 9 cm across the rim and 5 cm tall, with walls 7-8 mm thick.
Repeat for the second half. Both halves should match in rim diameter and depth. Set both face-down to check they are even.
Joining and shaping the body
Use
score-and-slip
on both rims. Press the two halves together to form a sphere, holding for 20 seconds. Roll the joined ball gently between your palms to smooth the equator seam.
Shape the front: squeeze one end of the sphere into a rounded, slightly tapered snout shape. The whale head is large and blunt, not sharply pointed. The widest part of the body sits behind the head.

Shape the rear: squeeze the opposite end into a narrowing tail peduncle, roughly 2-3 cm in diameter at the narrowest point. This is where the tail fluke will attach. Press the belly of the form against a flat surface to create a gently flattened underside so the whale sits stably.

Use a wooden rib to refine the body profile: blend the seam line on the belly, smooth the back, and define the head shape. The body at this point should be about 13 cm from nose to the tail peduncle tip.
Cutting and attaching the fins and tail
Roll the remaining 60 g of clay to a slab 5 mm thick. Cut the following shapes with a fettling knife using card templates:

Tail fluke: a horizontal crescent shape 8 cm wide and 3 cm deep from front to back curve, with a shallow notch cut at the centre of the rear edge. The two lobes of the fluke should curve gently upward at their tips.
Pectoral fins (two): long narrow triangles, each 5 cm long and 2 cm wide at the base, tapering to a rounded tip. These attach to the lower sides of the body behind the head.
Dorsal fin (one): a triangular shape 3 cm tall and 3 cm wide at its base, with a gently curved leading edge and a straighter trailing edge.

Score and slip each fin attachment point on the body and the base of the fin piece. Press each fin firmly in place. Blend the base of each fin into the body with a wooden rib so the join is smooth and the fin appears to grow from the body surface.

The tail fluke attaches to the narrow tail peduncle at the rear. Score and slip both the peduncle tip and the notched centre of the fluke. Press together and blend the join on both the top and underside of the peduncle.
Adding surface detail

This whale figurine is about 16 cm from nose to tail and 8 cm wide. It sits on a shelf or windowsill as a display piece. Make the body from two pinch pot halves. Join them at the belly seam and shape the front into an elongated point. Taper the rear into a tail. Cut the tail fluke, two side fins, and a dorsal fin from a thin slab. Press them on. No kiln is needed. The figurine dries at room temperature in two days.
Press two small dot indentations on the head for the blowhole (slightly off-centre toward the left when viewed from above). Use a needle tool tip.
Score fine parallel lines across the underside of the tail fluke lobes with a needle tool to suggest the natural ridging.
Drying

Set the whale on its belly on a flat board. The fins and tail fluke are the thinnest parts and will dry fastest. Cover loosely with a cloth for the first 12 to 18 hours to slow surface drying and give the body time to catch up. After the cloth is removed, the piece reaches
leather-hard
in eight to twelve hours: at this stage, refine any rough edges with a wooden rib. Full drying to
bone-dry
takes 48 hours for this size of piece.
Painting and sealing

Paint the upper body and dorsal surface with a deep blue-grey acrylic. Paint the belly area from chin to tail with white or pale cream, following the lateral line scored into the clay. Allow to dry, then apply a second coat. Add very faint dark blue streaks along the back for shading depth. Paint two small dark dots for eyes, positioned on the sides of the head just behind the snout tip. Once the paint is dry, apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to seal all surfaces.
Use and care

This whale is a decorative figurine for indoor use. Air-dry clay is not waterproof: keep it away from moisture. The fins, dorsal fin, and tail fluke are the most vulnerable parts: handle by the body. Dust with a dry brush. Do not wash by immersion.
Variations
Build the whale in paper clay air-dry for a stronger form that is less prone to fin breakage. Paper clay also accepts finer surface scoring for gill lines and body markings.
Make a dolphin variant using the same two-joined-pinch-pot body but shaping a more pointed rostrum, a smaller dorsal fin, and a narrower tail. Paint in grey with a white belly.

Create a sea-life group. Make a large whale, a medium dolphin, and two smaller fish. Shape the fish from flattened pinch pots with tail and fin attachments. Arrange all four on a shared slab base. Paint the base in blue and white.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Fins crack away from the body during drying
items.cause: The fin attachments dried faster than the body, pulling the join open
items.fix: Cover with a cloth for the first 18 hours. If a fin breaks at bone-dry, reattach with PVA glue rather than clay slip

items.problem: Body seam is visible as a raised ridge around the belly
items.cause: The equator seam was not smoothed thoroughly when the two halves were joined
items.fix: At leather-hard, press the seam flat with a wooden rib and smooth with a barely damp sponge. If the seam is already bone-dry, sand it lightly and fill with acrylic paint

items.problem: Tail fluke droops downward during drying
items.cause: The fluke was too thin or attached while the clay at the peduncle was still very soft
items.fix: Support the underside of the tail fluke with a small rolled-clay prop or a folded tissue while it dries. Remove the support once the clay has firmed to leather-hard

items.problem: Body cracks across the widest section
items.cause: The joined sphere was not fully hollow: if the walls were too thick, trapped air and uneven drying cause cracks
items.fix: Ensure walls are 7-8 mm thick throughout pinching. A consistent wall thickness dries evenly. Small cracks at leather-hard can be filled with fresh slip; bone-dry cracks fill with diluted PVA pressed in with a brush
